newsitem.title: UK: Pound to regain poise after Labour landslide win.
newsitem.headline: Pound to regain poise after Labour landslide win.

text.p: Sterling's shaky performance on Friday in the wake of Labour's landslide victory in the British election merely reflects the market's drive to take profits rather than a change in trend, currency analysts said.

The fundamental factors that boosted the pound to 4-1/2-year highs against the mark last month are still in place. Unless the new government embarks on a completely different economic course than promised before the election, sterling is still a buy for many traders.

"The new goverment will underline its credibility to the financial markets by raising interest rates very soon," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS in London. "The market went into the election very long of sterling and sold once it got the news."

"Unless there is a fundamental change in the policies the Labour party proposed before the election, the pound is likely to recover," he said. "Downmoves like today should be seen as a buying opportunity."
Much of sterling's sizzling rally of about 25 percent against the mark since August has been due to speculative flows by investors betting on further rises in UK interest rates.

The benefit of the landslide victory is that the party will not have to court its more left-wing politicians to retain power and can keep the skeletons of its high-spending and taxing past in the cupboard, analysts said.

Labour leader Tony Blair has thoroughly reformed the party, and analysts expect the finance minister-in-waiting Gordon Brown to stick to his election promise of reining in public spending and keeping a tight grip on inflation.
Brown said overnight a Labour government would deliver its first budget within two months and would set monetary policy to meet an inflation target of 2.5 percent.
"Blair has good support among the modernisers, and so the old guard of Labour leftists is unlikely to rock the boat," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in London.

The magnitude of Labour's victory, forecast to result in a majority of 179 seats in parliament, might not be entirely welcome in the markets as it means there will be few checks on government policy, Fox said.
Market concern that Labour might adopt policies to ease the burden on exporters and weaken the strong pound were highlighted by an article in the Times newspaper today.
The editorial article called for a policy of gradual currency depreciation to avoid further economic damage from a strong pound and also recommended fiscal tightening.

"The fact that markets are reacting to this extent to such a story illustrates, ..., how much uncertainty there actually is about what kind of policies Labour wants to pursue," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

If fiscal tighening rather than interest rate rises were to move to the top of the Labour Party's economic agenda, the pound would be deprived of the attraction of higher interest rates, the main engine behind its rally.

A quarter of a percentage point rise in British base rates is widely expected at the next monetary meeting, which is scheduled for May 7 but might be postponed because of its proximity to the election.
The pound shed over three pfennigs from pre-election result levels and was down two cents in European morning trading on Friday but recovered from the lows as bargain-hunters stepped into the market.

At 1030 GMT the pound was at 2.7810/20 marks, down from 2.7970/90 before the election result but well above a low at 2.7560. Against the dollar it was at $1.6122/43 against a low at $1.6008 and $1.6253/60 before the poll results.
